procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated as Writ Petitions Nos. 109 to 114, 117, 118, 120, 121, 128 to 133, 142, 143, 186, 190 and 191 of 1967 filed directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The petitioners challenged an order of detention passed against them under Rule 30(1)(b) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text. The case was directly filed in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court dismissed the petitions.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order made by the President under Article 359(1) is a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and can be tested against the fundamental rights in Part III, including the very fundamental right whose enforcement it suspends.

law.name: Article 359(1) of the Constitution
law.description: Allows the President, during a Proclamation of Emergency, to issue an order suspending the right to move any court for the enforcement of specified fundamental rights.

law.name: Article 13(2) of the Constitution
law.description: Prohibits the State from making any 'law' which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III (Fundamental Rights).

application.description: The Court applied the principle of 'harmonious construction'. It stated that both Article 13(2) and Article 359 are parts of the same Constitution, stand on equal footing, and must be read together in a way that gives effect to both, rather than allowing one to nullify the other.

The Court reasoned that if a Presidential order under Article 359 were treated as a 'law' under Article 13(2), it would create a logical contradiction. The order, which is meant to suspend the enforcement of a fundamental right, could then be challenged for violating the very same fundamental right it suspends.

The Court described this scenario as "arguing in a circle" and concluded that it would make Article 359 "completely nugatory" (useless or ineffective). The entire purpose of Article 359 is to allow for the temporary suspension of the enforcement of these rights during an emergency.

Therefore, the Court held that while a Presidential order might be considered a 'law' in its widest sense, it cannot be a 'law' for the specific purpose of Article 13(2). To hold otherwise would defeat the clear constitutional intent behind Article 359.
The Court explicitly stated that an order under Article 359 derives its force from the article itself and cannot be tested against the provisions of Part III that it is designed to suspend.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument. It held that an order made by the President under Article 359(1) cannot be considered a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2). Consequently, such an order cannot be tested for its validity against the very fundamental right whose enforcement it suspends, as doing so would render Article 359 nugatory.

issue.issue_text: Whether the President's order under Article 359 was violative of Article 14 as it enabled the executive to exercise arbitrary discretion in choosing between the Defence of India Act and the Preventive Detention Act for detaining a person.

facts: During a Proclamation of Emergency, the President issued an order under Article 359 of the Constitution.
This order suspended the right to move any court for the enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 21, and 22 for any person deprived of such rights under the Defence of India Act.
The petitioners argued that this order violated Article 14 (the right to equality).

Their specific claim was that the order gave the executive arbitrary discretion to detain some people under the more 'drastic' Defence of India Act, while others could be detained under the Preventive Detention Act, creating a discriminatory situation.
law: Article 359 of the Constitution empowers the President to suspend the enforcement of fundamental rights during an emergency.
Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees the right to equality before the law.
application: The Court pointed out that the President's order, which was being challenged, was the very instrument that suspended the enforcement of Article 14.
The core of the petitioners' argument was a challenge based on Article 14.
The Court reasoned that since the right to enforce Article 14 was itself suspended by the President's order, that same order could not be challenged on the grounds that it violated Article 14.

The Court stated that even assuming the Defence of India Act's provisions were more stringent, the suspension of Article 14 meant that no legal question of the order being 'bad under Art. 14' could arise.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that because the President's order under Article 359 had validly suspended the enforcement of the fundamental right under Article 14, the order itself could not be challenged for being violative of Article 14.

issue.issue_text: Whether an express provision in the Defence of India Act and its Rules, stating that the enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 21, and 22 was suspended, is necessary for the Presidential order under Article 359 to be effective.

facts: During a Proclamation of Emergency, the President issued an order under Article 359 of the Constitution.

This order suspended the right of any person to move a court for the enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 21, and 22, if they were deprived of such rights under the Defence of India Act or its Rules.

The petitioners argued that for this Presidential order to be effective, the Defence of India Act itself (or its Rules) should have contained an express provision stating that the enforcement of these fundamental rights was suspended.
law: Article 359(1) of the Constitution grants the President the power to suspend the enforcement of fundamental rights during an emergency.
An Act of Parliament or its Rules cannot, by themselves, suspend fundamental rights, as such a provision would be unconstitutional.
application: The Supreme Court found the petitioner's argument to be fundamentally flawed.
The Court reasoned that if the Defence of India Act or its Rules contained a provision suspending fundamental rights, that provision itself would be unconstitutional.
The power to suspend the *enforcement* of fundamental rights is a unique constitutional power granted exclusively to the President under Article 359(1) during an emergency.

The Presidential order did not require the Act to have a corresponding provision. Instead, the order's clear intent was to bar any legal challenge based on Articles 14, 21, and 22 against actions taken *under the authority of* the Defence of India Act.
Therefore, the Presidential order was sufficient on its own to suspend the enforcement of these rights in relation to detentions under the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that it was not necessary for the Defence of India Act or its Rules to contain an express provision suspending the enforcement of fundamental rights. The Court clarified that such a provision in the Act would be unconstitutional, as the power to suspend the enforcement of rights during an emergency rests solely with the President under Article 359 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the requirement to furnish grounds of detention under Article 22(5) persists even after the President's order suspended the enforcement of Article 22.

facts: A Presidential order was issued that suspended the enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 22.
The petitioners (detenus) contended that the requirement under Article 22(5) to be provided with the grounds for their detention must still be applicable, despite the President's order.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution states that when any person is detained, the authority making the order shall communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made.
application: The Court found this argument incomprehensible.
It reasoned that the President's order, which it held to be valid, suspended the enforcement of the entirety of Article 22.
Since Article 22(5) is only a part (a clause) of Article 22, it cannot continue to be in effect when the whole article has been suspended.
The suspension of the whole article necessarily includes the suspension of all its parts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention, holding that since the President's order validly suspended the enforcement of the entire Article 22, the requirement to furnish grounds of detention under Article 22(5) was also suspended.

issue.issue_text: Whether the detention order by the Jammu & Kashmir Government was invalid for not being in the form required by Article 166 of the Constitution of India.

facts: The petitioner argued that a detention order issued by the Jammu & Kashmir Government was invalid.
The basis for this argument was that the order was not in the form required by Article 166 of the Constitution of India.
law: The Supreme Court established that Article 166 of the Constitution of India does not apply to the State of Jammu & Kashmir.
The correct legal provision to assess the form of such an order is Section 45 of the Constitution of Jammu & Kashmir.
application: The Court examined the detention order and found that it was in the form required by Section 45 of the Constitution of Jammu & Kashmir.
Because the order complied with the applicable law (Section 45), the Court made a presumption that it was passed validly.
The Court noted that the petitioner had not made any attempt to show that the order was not passed as required by law, thus failing to rebut this presumption of validity.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that the detention order was not invalid because the relevant law was Section 45 of the Jammu & Kashmir Constitution, not Article 166 of the Indian Constitution, and the order complied with that requirement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order made by the President under Article 359(1) is a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and can be tested against the fundamental rights in Part III, including the very fundamental right whose enforcement it suspends.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's argument, as inferred from the respondent's counter-argument, is that the President's order under Article 359 is a 'law' and can be tested against the very fundamental right whose enforcement it suspends.
respondent_arguments: Once the President has passed an order under Art. 359 suspending the enforcement of any fundamental right, it is not open to rely on that fundamental right for any purpose.
An order under Art. 359 cannot be tested in any manner by the very fundamental right the enforcement of which it has suspended.

cases.principle: A Presidential order under Art. 359 can be restricted in scope to a class of persons, provided the operation of the order is confined to an area and a period. The court clarified this does not permit a broad challenge to the suspension order itself under Art. 14, except in theoretical cases of mala fide action or clear abuse of power.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order issued by the President under Article 359 of the Constitution, which suspends the enforcement of fundamental rights, cannot be considered 'law' for the purposes of Article 13(2) and cannot be tested against the very rights it suspends. When such an order suspends the entirety of a fundamental right, such as Article 22, all its constituent clauses, including procedural requirements like providing grounds for detention under Article 22(5), are also suspended. Furthermore, Article 166 of the Constitution of India does not apply to the State of Jammu & Kashmir; the validity of an executive order there is to be determined by the Constitution of Jammu & Kashmir.
obiter: We may assume for present purposes that the President is comprised within the word 'State' in Art. 12.
We may also assume that the order made by the President under Art. 359 is a law in its widest sense.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central conclusion is that a Presidential order under Article 359(1) suspending the enforcement of specified fundamental rights during an Emergency creates an absolute bar against invoking those rights in court for any purpose. Such an order cannot be challenged on the grounds that it violates the very rights it suspends, and any action taken under the laws specified in the order is immune from judicial scrutiny based on those suspended rights. The power to suspend flows directly and exclusively from the Constitution via the President's order, and the necessity of such a suspension for the security of India is implicit in the constitutional provision itself and does not require separate justification.
legal_tests_applied: Constitutional Interpretation of Article 359: The court applied a textual and purposive interpretation, holding that the article's language is unambiguous and its purpose is to allow the President to suspend the enforcement of any fundamental right deemed necessary for the security of India during an emergency.

Jurisdictional Bar: The court treated the Presidential order under Article 359 as creating a jurisdictional bar, preventing courts from entertaining any challenge based on the suspended fundamental rights against actions taken under the specified emergency laws.

Constitutional Applicability Test: The court determined the validity of the detention order by examining which constitution (Constitution of India or Constitution of Jammu & Kashmir) applied to the executive action in question.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the President's order under Article 359 could be tested against the very fundamental right it suspends was rejected because once enforcement is suspended, the right cannot be relied upon for any purpose, including to challenge the suspension itself.

The challenge that the President's order was violative of Article 14 failed because the enforcement of Article 14 itself was suspended. The court reasoned: 'As the enforcement of the fundamental right under Art. 14 was suspended by the President's order under Art. 359, no question of that order being bad under that Article can arise.'

The contention that the Defence of India Act required an express provision suspending fundamental rights was dismissed as constitutionally unsound. The court stated, 'Such a provision in the Act or the Rules would be clearly unconstitutional. It is only because Art. 359(1) provides that the President may suspend the enforcement of a particular fundamental right that it is possible for the enforcement of any fundamental right to be suspended during the Emergency.'

The challenge to the form of the detention order under Article 166 of the Constitution of India was rejected because the court found that Article 166 was not applicable. The court held: 'It is enough to say that Art. 166 does not apply to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. We .have to look to the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir to see whether the form of the order is in accordance therewith. It is clear that the order is in the form required by s. 45 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir.'

The claim that the requirement to furnish grounds under Article 22(5) persists was implicitly rejected, as the President's order suspended the enforcement of the entirety of Article 22, thereby barring any legal action to enforce any of its clauses.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's argument that 'once the President has passed an order under Art. 359 suspending the enforcement of any fundamental right, it is not open to rely on that fundamental right for any purpose... and such an order cannot be'testcd in any manner by the very fundamental right the enforcement· of which it has suspended.'

The respondent prevailed on the Article 14 issue because the suspension of the right to enforce Article 14 by the President's order was held to be a complete answer to any challenge based on that article.

The respondent's position was upheld that the suspension's legal force comes directly from the President's order under Article 359, not from any provision within the Defence of India Act. The court affirmed that the Act could not and did not need to contain its own suspension clause.

The respondent successfully argued that the detention order was valid because it conformed to the requirements of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, which was the correct legal framework to apply, not Article 166 of the Constitution of India.
policy_considerations: The court heavily relied on the policy of national security embedded within Article 359. It stated, 'Article 359 itself posits that it may be necessary in the interest of the security of India to pass an order suspending the enforcement of any fundamental right thereunder.' The court further reasoned that this is a 'basic assumption' and 'it is unnecessary in the face of that basic assumption to inquire whether enforcement of a particular fundamental right suspended by the President has anything to do with the security of India, for that is implicit in Art. 359.'
